appraisal_events.evidence: "Faut-il que ce pauvre M. Vinteuil soit aveuglé par la tendresse... permettre à sa fille... de faire vivre sous son toit une femme pareille"; docteur Percepied's mocking retelling "savait faire rire aux larmes le curé et tout le monde"
appraisal_events.explanation: Village gossip, epitomized by Percepied's crude jokes, blames Vinteuil for tolerating his daughter's disreputable companion and openly mocks the household.

appraisal_events.evidence: il se voyait avec sa fille dans le dernier bas-fond, et ses manières en avaient reçu depuis peu cette humilité, ce respect pour ceux qui se trouvaient au-dessus de lui
appraisal_events.explanation: Internalizing the village's judgment, Vinteuil comes to see himself and his daughter as socially bottom-ranked, and his manner visibly takes on new deference toward his superiors.

appraisal_events.evidence: Swann... avait longuement causé avec M. Vinteuil... et lui avait demandé... s'il n'enverrait pas un jour sa fille jouer à Tansonville. — "Quel homme exquis," nous dit-il... avec la même enthousiaste vénération
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann's unprecedented, if narrated as self-flatteringly condescending, kindness toward Vinteuil earns him effusive admiration and gratitude.

appraisal_events.evidence: mes parents déplorèrent avec M. Vinteuil le mariage de Swann au nom de principes et de convenances... "Quel malheur qu'il ait fait un mariage tout à fait déplacé."
appraisal_events.explanation: Even while admiring Swann personally, the narrator's parents and Vinteuil join in socially condemning his marriage, a hypocrisy the narrator explicitly notes.

status_effects.explanation: He is mocked and blamed by village gossip for tolerating his daughter's companion.
Her conduct is the explicit subject of the village's mocking rumor.
She is described as having a bad reputation in the area and is the target of the household's scandal.
His standing visibly collapses: he now carries himself with a new, witnessed deference toward those he considers above him.
Vinteuil praises Swann as an exquisite man with enthusiastic veneration.
Swann's overture toward him, previously never so much as addressed, functions as an honorable, valued support he is almost afraid to use.
His marriage is publicly deplored as unsuitable even by those who esteem him personally, marking a witnessed social discredit.

ambiguities: The passage explicitly flags the hypocrisy of the narrator's parents and Vinteuil praising Swann personally while condemning his marriage socially, immediately after Vinteuil's admiring exclamation.
